q: How long does meth stay in the blood?
short: After the blood level peaks, it takes about 10 to 12 hours to fall by half.

q: How fast do the effects of a snorted dose peak?
short: Snorted, its effects on the heart and on mood peak within about 15 minutes.

q: What does meth do in the brain?
short: It makes nerve cells let out three brain chemicals: dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin.

q: How much reaches the blood when it is snorted or smoked?
short: Most of a snorted dose reaches the blood. For smoking, the figures vary a lot.

q: Do the two mirror-image forms of meth act differently?
short: Yes: in one study, the 'l' form felt weaker and its effects ended sooner.

q: What does one dose of meth do to the body and mood?
short: One snorted dose raises heart rate and blood pressure and makes people feel high.

q: Does one dose of meth make thinking worse at the time?
short: In lab tests, single doses did not measurably worsen attention or memory.

q: Do meth's effects fade while it is still in the blood?
short: The good feelings fade within one dose and within three days; hunger stays gone.

q: Does meth reduce appetite?
short: One dose cut how much people ate that day by about two fifths.

q: What does meth poisoning look like?
short: Meth poisoning can look like a body in overdrive: a racing heart, fast breathing, being very restless and upset.

q: How many people who use stimulants like meth become dependent?
short: An old US survey asked people who had used stimulants like meth. About 11 in 100 had been dependent at some point.

q: Do people who use meth always pick the drug over cash?
short: In lab choice tests, people often chose small amounts of cash over a stimulant dose.

q: What is meth withdrawal like, and how long does it last?
short: After stopping, most symptoms people reported eased within one to two weeks. Low mood and craving lasted longer.

q: Does meth damage dopamine nerve cells?
short: Nobody has shown either way whether meth, as people use it, damages dopamine nerve cells.

q: Is the dopamine system different in people who used meth heavily?
short: People who used meth heavily have less of one dopamine protein on scans than people who don't, on average.

q: Do dopamine changes in people who used meth recover after stopping?
short: In five people, that protein rose after a year without meth.

q: What do scans of the brain's dopamine-storage protein show after meth?
short: A few days after use, another dopamine marker looks higher. After about 10 days off meth, it is not clearly different.

q: Do people who used meth have less grey matter?
short: Some brain areas looked smaller soon after stopping. Other studies found some larger.

q: Is brain activity different in people who have stopped using meth?
short: The results are mixed: the differences found were small, uncertain or not repeated.

q: Does brain activity change after a year without meth?
short: In five people, one deep brain area got more active after a year off meth, compared with the rest of the brain.

q: Could brain differences seen in stimulant dependence be there before drug use?
short: Brothers and sisters who never had drug or alcohol problems shared some brain differences with their sibling dependent on stimulants.

q: Is meth linked to Parkinson's disease?
short: Parkinson's was diagnosed more often in people with a meth or amphetamine diagnosis and no other drug or alcohol diagnosis.

q: Do people dependent on meth score lower on memory and thinking tests?
short: On average, people dependent on meth score somewhat lower on memory and thinking tests than healthy volunteers.

q: Are thinking-test scores of people dependent on meth in the normal range?
short: On average, their scores were in the normal range, not the impaired range.

q: Does meth cause lasting problems with thinking and memory?
short: It has not been shown that meth causes lasting problems with thinking and memory in people.

q: Do memory and thinking get better after stopping meth?
short: We don't know yet. In retests, people who stopped did not clearly improve more than people who don't use.

q: Is meth linked to psychosis?
short: Psychotic symptoms are more common in people who use meth, most of all in those who use it often.

q: In people dependent on meth, is frequent use linked to psychotic symptoms?
short: In people dependent on meth, psychotic symptoms were much more common in months of heavy use.

q: How long does meth-related psychosis last?
short: In a typical study of people with meth psychosis, about 1 in 4 still had symptoms over a month after stopping.

q: How does meth psychosis compare with schizophrenia?
short: Meth psychosis and schizophrenia can look alike.

q: Is meth linked to depression?
short: People who use meth report low mood somewhat more often than people who don't.

q: Is meth use linked to suicidal thoughts and attempts?
short: People with a meth use disorder report suicidal thoughts and attempts more often.

q: Is meth linked to violence?
short: Two long-term studies linked meth use to more violence. This held after other things were counted.

q: Does naltrexone with bupropion help people stay off meth during treatment?
short: In one big trial, for every 9 people given two medicines, about 1 more had mostly meth-free urine tests.

q: Does the antidepressant mirtazapine help people use less meth?
short: In three trials, people on a depression medicine, mirtazapine, used somewhat less meth than on a dummy pill.

q: Do bupropion or modafinil help people stop using meth?
short: Bupropion and modafinil did not help more people stop than a dummy pill.

q: Do any medicines ease meth withdrawal?
short: No medicine on sale has clearly been shown to ease meth withdrawal.

q: Have any medicines been shown to help meth psychosis?
short: Few trials have tested medicines for meth psychosis: eight small, short ones and one longer one.

q: How many people who use meth or amphetamine regularly die each year?
short: Among people with regular or problematic use, about 1 in 90 died each year.

q: Have meth use and meth deaths risen in the US?
short: In the US, meth use rose from 2015 to 2019, and deaths involving meth kept rising through 2023, the latest year counted.

q: Is a serotonin by-product lower in people who use MDMA?
short: In one study, a serotonin by-product in spinal fluid was lower in people who used MDMA.

q: Do people who use ecstasy score lower on memory tests?
short: On average, people who use ecstasy score lower on some memory and thinking tests.

q: Are lower memory scores due to ecstasy, or to other drugs?
short: In people who used ecstasy but hardly any other drug, memory scores were no different.

q: Does memory change when people start using ecstasy?
short: In one Dutch study, people who started using ecstasy improved less on a word-memory test.

q: Does memory recover after people stop using ecstasy?
short: Nobody knows yet whether scores recover after people stop using ecstasy.

q: Do brain scans show serotonin changes in people who use ecstasy?
short: Scans show less of a serotonin marker in people who use ecstasy.

q: What happened to the famous 2002 study claiming ecstasy damaged monkeys' brains?
short: A 2002 study said ecstasy harmed monkeys' brains. It was withdrawn a year later.

q: Does ecstasy damage dopamine nerve cells?
short: It has not been shown that ecstasy harms dopamine nerve cells in people.

q: Does ecstasy harm the brain for good?
short: Experts disagree about whether ecstasy leaves lasting harm to the serotonin system.

q: Is meth use linked to crime?
short: People dependent on meth reported more crime in months when they used it.

q: Does MDMA-assisted therapy help PTSD more than therapy with a dummy pill?
short: With the same therapy, PTSD scores fell more with MDMA than with a dummy pill.

q: Could people in the trials tell if they got MDMA?
short: In the trial that asked, most people could tell MDMA from the dummy pill.

q: What side effects did MDMA cause in the PTSD trials?
short: MDMA often gave brief side effects, like tight muscles, feeling sick and sweating.

q: Did the US regulator approve MDMA therapy for PTSD in 2024?
short: In 2024 the US drug regulator said no to MDMA therapy for PTSD.

q: Why were three earlier MDMA therapy studies withdrawn?
short: In 2024 a journal withdrew three earlier studies from the MDMA therapy research.

q: Is MDMA therapy good value for money?
short: Two critics say price and comparison decide if MDMA therapy is good value.

q: Do the MDMA therapy trials hold up?
short: Whether MDMA itself helps PTSD, and for how long, is not settled.

q: Does the benefit of MDMA therapy for PTSD last?
short: Months to years later, people who had MDMA still scored lower on PTSD.

q: Does MDMA therapy help people with alcohol problems?
short: In one small study, 9 of 14 people drank much less after MDMA therapy.

q: Does MDMA therapy ease anxiety in people with a serious illness?
short: In one small trial, anxiety fell more with MDMA than with a dummy pill.

q: Does MDMA therapy help social anxiety in autistic adults?
short: In one small trial, social anxiety eased more with MDMA than with a dummy pill.

q: Does MDMA therapy help couples where one partner has PTSD?
short: After couples therapy with MDMA, PTSD eased and couples were happier.

q: Does MDMA therapy help depression?
short: In one small study, depression dropped a lot after two MDMA sessions.

q: Did MDMA therapy for PTSD change people's drinking or drug use?
short: MDMA therapy for PTSD did not clearly change drinking or drug use.

q: What side effects did MDMA cause in trials outside PTSD?
short: In small trials, MDMA's side effects were common and brief, and none were serious.

q: In the early MDMA trials for PTSD, did the benefit last?
short: In two sets of early PTSD trials, average PTSD scores stayed about as low as at the end of MDMA therapy a year or more later.

q: Does MDMA therapy for PTSD change sleep?
short: In early PTSD trials, people who had full doses of MDMA said they slept better than people who had a very small dose.

q: Across all MDMA therapy trials, which side effects were common?
short: In trials, MDMA often caused side effects such as a tight jaw, worry, less appetite or feeling sick, mostly gone within a week.

q: What else has MDMA therapy been tried for?
short: Outside PTSD, nobody can yet say whether MDMA therapy helps.

q: How was MDMA used in therapy before it was banned?
short: Before MDMA was banned in 1985, a few dozen US therapists used it in talking therapy.

q: What happens when meth and alcohol are taken together?
short: With alcohol, meth raises the heart rate more and makes people feel less drunk.

q: Does a second dose work like the first?
short: A second dose raises the drug in your blood, but not the strongest feeling.

q: Does MDMA stop working as well with regular use?
short: Most people who keep using ecstasy say it stops working as well.

q: What does a second dose do to the heart and body?
short: Taking more adds strain on the heart and blood pressure without stronger good feelings.

q: Opioids with benzodiazepines: how much riskier?
short: People on prescribed opioids and benzos had more overdoses than people on opioids alone.

q: How many opioid deaths also involve benzodiazepines?
short: About 1 in 5 US opioid overdose deaths in 2017 also involved benzos.

q: How many opioid deaths also involve alcohol?
short: Alcohol was listed in about 1 in 7 US opioid overdose deaths.

q: On methadone or buprenorphine and also prescribed sedatives?
short: In UK methadone or buprenorphine treatment, benzo prescriptions were linked to more poisoning deaths.

q: Is the change bigger in people who have used more?
short: People who had taken more ecstasy showed less of the serotonin marker.

q: After stopping ecstasy, do serotonin changes on scans return to normal?
short: We do not know if the marker goes back to normal after people stop.

q: Do brain scans change when people first start using ecstasy?
short: In one study, a few pills did not change the serotonin marker.

q: Opioids with gabapentin or pregabalin: how much riskier?
short: Gabapentin or pregabalin with opioid painkillers was linked to more opioid overdose deaths in Ontario.

q: What does MDMA do to body temperature, heart and blood pressure?
short: In a laboratory, one dose of MDMA raised blood pressure, heart rate and temperature.
topic: What it does to the body

q: Why do some people overheat on MDMA?
short: Nobody can yet say why some people get hotter than others with MDMA.
topic: What it does to the body

q: Can drinking lots of water on MDMA lead to low blood salt?
short: Some young people were treated for low blood salt (sodium) after taking MDMA.
topic: What it does to the body

q: Is low blood salt after MDMA more common in women?
short: Women with MDMA illness more often had low blood salt than men did.
topic: What it does to the body

q: What can MDMA do to the kidneys?
short: Kidney injury after MDMA has been reported in single cases; nobody knows how often.
topic: What it does to the body

q: Is ecstasy really MDMA, and how strong are the pills?
short: Ecstasy pills are often MDMA, but not always, and the amount varies a lot.

q: Can people become dependent on ecstasy?
short: Some people become dependent on ecstasy. Studies disagree on how many.

q: Can regular heavy MDMA use harm the heart valves?
short: Heart valve changes were more common in people who had taken MDMA, in one small study.
topic: What it does to the body

q: In MDMA deaths, which medicines were found too?
short: Among 19 Australian deaths with MDMA and a risky mix, antidepressants, opioids and benzos were common.

q: What is serotonin syndrome, and how do doctors spot it?
short: Doctors look for muscle jerks, shaking, sweating and restlessness when serotonin may be too high.

q: What about MAOI antidepressants, like moclobemide?
short: Four young people in Finland died with MDMA and moclobemide, an antidepressant, in their blood.

q: What about other drugs that raise serotonin?
short: One 2007 review ranked drugs by serotonin risk with ecstasy: MAOIs highest, SSRIs lower.

q: Opioid painkillers with MAOI antidepressants?
short: Reports link pethidine and tramadol to bad reactions with MAOI antidepressants; none for morphine.

q: What happens when cocaine and alcohol are used together?
short: Together they make a new substance, cocaethylene, and hearts beat faster than with cocaine alone.

q: Can cocaine make someone feel less drunk?
short: People given cocaine with alcohol did not feel more drunk, and sometimes slightly less.

q: Why can the usual amount be dangerous after a break?
short: Two reviews say tolerance to opioids may fall after a break from using them.

q: What happens with SSRI antidepressants?
short: An SSRI muted MDMA's effects in lab tests; with paroxetine, MDMA blood levels rose.

q: What about other antidepressants?
short: Other antidepressants did not act alike: some muted MDMA's effects, and bupropion did not.

q: What do case reports say about mixing with medicines?
short: In safety reports, ecstasy cases that also named an antidepressant ended in death more often.

q: What about other psychiatric medicines?
short: Few other psychiatric medicines were tested with MDMA, and the results differ by medicine.

q: Why do some bodies, or some medicines, make MDMA stronger?
short: MDMA seems to switch off the enzyme that clears it, so body differences matter less.

q: Why does taking more raise blood levels more than expected?
short: A bigger dose of MDMA raised blood levels by more than the dose itself rose.

q: Is using ecstasy in pregnancy linked to birth defects?
short: One study counted birth defects after ecstasy in pregnancy, but it cannot show cause.

q: How do babies exposed to ecstasy in pregnancy do in their first months?
short: At 1 and 4 months, babies of women who used ecstasy mostly scored the same.

q: Cannabis with alcohol: is driving worse than with either alone?
short: Cannabis with alcohol was linked to worse driving, about the sum of each.

q: Cannabis alone: are drivers who test positive more often in crashes?
short: Drivers with cannabis in a test were linked to more crashes.

q: GHB or GBL with alcohol: what changes?
short: People who took GHB with alcohol were less awake more often at hospital.

q: What does MDMA feel like?
short: Compared with a dummy pill, lab MDMA felt good for hours, with unwanted effects too.

q: Do nicotine patches and gum help people stop smoking?
short: Nicotine patches, gum and similar help people who want to stop smoking.

q: What does smoking cannabis do to the lungs?
short: Smoking cannabis is linked to cough, phlegm and wheeze; light smoking didn't lower lung function.

q: Are edibles a danger to young children?
short: Calls to US poison centres about young children eating edibles rose about 15 times over, 2017 to 2021.

q: What does a hangover do to my thinking the next day?
short: The morning after heavy drinking, people remembered less and reacted slower than on alcohol-free days.

q: Do I drive worse the morning after, even with no alcohol left?
short: Young drivers in a lab driving test drove worse after drinking nights than after alcohol-free nights.

q: Does drinking water while drinking alcohol stop a hangover?
short: In one small test, men felt no better next morning when they had water between drinks than when they drank the same sake without it.

q: Does mixing caffeine with alcohol change my hangover?
short: People who drank beer with added caffeine had about the same hangover as those without caffeine.

q: Does drinking beer before wine, or wine before beer, change my hangover?
short: Drinking beer before wine or wine before beer gave about the same hangover.

q: Do people who take hangover pills drink more?
short: Young adults who had used hangover pills reported more drinking problems than those who never had.

q: Does paracetamol at usual doses harm the liver in people who drink?
short: In short trials, paracetamol at usual doses did not raise a liver test more than dummy pills; some trials saw small, short-lived rises later.

q: Is there a medicine that makes amphetamine withdrawal easier?
short: In the four trials reviewed, no medicine clearly eased withdrawal or craving more than a dummy pill.

q: Does meth taken during the day spoil that night's sleep?
short: After one of the larger doses, people slept less and worse that night than after a dummy dose.

q: How do you feel the morning after one dose of meth?
short: Next morning, the biggest dose left people less alert and friendly than a dummy dose.

q: Does exercise help low mood and worry after stopping meth?
short: In one trial, exercise went with slightly less sadness and worry than health classes.

q: Does exercise make the urge to use meth weaker?
short: Studies report less craving with exercise than without, but the review that lists them does not say how much less.

q: How does sleep change in the weeks after stopping cocaine?
short: Over three weeks off cocaine, measured sleep got worse while people felt they slept better.

q: Can the medicine modafinil help sleep after stopping cocaine?
short: In one small trial, modafinil helped people fall asleep faster than a dummy pill did.

q: Do clonidine or lofexidine help with opioid withdrawal?
short: Yes: compared with a dummy pill, fewer people had bad withdrawal and more finished treatment.

q: Is clonidine as good as slowly cutting down methadone for coming off opioids?
short: No clear difference in how many people finished, but clonidine-type medicines caused more low blood pressure and other side effects.

q: Does buprenorphine help people get through opioid withdrawal better than clonidine?
short: Yes: more people finished withdrawal treatment with buprenorphine than with clonidine or lofexidine.

q: Is buprenorphine better than slowly cutting down methadone for coming off opioids?
short: They worked about the same: similar numbers of people finished withdrawal treatment with each.

q: Is withdrawal from fentanyl worse than from heroin or other opioids?
short: In one study, people coming off fentanyl had worse withdrawal than people coming off other opioids, such as heroin.

q: Does the ADHD medicine methylphenidate cause sleep problems?
short: Children on methylphenidate had sleep problems recorded more often than children on a dummy pill.

q: Does MDMA spoil sleep that night?
short: After MDMA, people slept about two hours less than with a dummy pill, and had very little dreaming (REM) sleep.

q: Are you sleepier the day after MDMA?
short: We don't know: next-day sleepiness after MDMA was not clearly different from a dummy pill.

q: After high doses of DXM, how long is balance affected?
short: After the highest doses, balance and coordination were still affected at the day's last test, while other effects were wearing off.

q: A month after high doses of DXM, any lasting effects?
short: A month later, no one reported lasting upset or lasting changes in what they saw or heard.

q: Will I sleep badly when I stop heroin or other opioids?
short: Studies in one review found shorter, lighter sleep in the first weeks after stopping heroin than in good sleepers.

q: Does alcohol help sleep, and what happens when I stop?
short: Alcohol can help people fall asleep at first, but studies in one review found long heavy drinking leaves sleep poor for months.

q: Will I sleep badly when I stop cannabis?
short: Studies in one review found that many people who used cannabis regularly sleep badly after stopping, often with strange dreams.

q: Can sleep medicines help when I stop alcohol, cannabis, cocaine or opioids?
short: Some helped sleep, but better sleep did not reliably help people stay off drugs.

q: How does GHB affect driving?
short: Soon after GHB, people crashed far more in a driving test than after a dummy drink.

q: Does GHB affect my memory or thinking afterwards?
short: GHB affects memory while it works; in one study, people who had passed out from GHB many times had worse memory than other people who used GHB or other drugs.

q: How do people feel in the days and weeks after a psychedelic?
short: Studies often found less low mood and stress than before, and more wellbeing; some people had headaches or slept badly.

q: Can I get flashbacks after LSD or psilocybin?
short: About 1 in 11 lab volunteers reported a short flashback, mostly in the days after.

q: Is it dangerous to take loperamide (Imodium) to get through opioid withdrawal?
short: It can be: some people who took very large amounts got serious heart-rhythm problems.

q: Do medicines for constipation caused by opioids work?
short: Yes: compared with a dummy pill, more people's constipation got better.

q: Why do some people on methadone feel withdrawal before their next dose?
short: In one small study, their methadone level tended to drop faster after its daily high point.

q: Can poppers damage your eyes?
short: It seems so, in some people: reports describe blurry central vision and damage at the back of the eye.

q: Can a benzodiazepine sleeping pill affect my driving the next day?
short: Some benzodiazepine sleeping pills made people drive worse the next day than after dummy pills.

q: Taken nightly, do benzodiazepine sleeping pills still impair driving the next morning?
short: For most pills the morning effect seemed smaller after several nights than after the first, but for some it lasted or grew over a week.

q: Am I more likely to crash or fall when I start sleeping pills?
short: Some studies found more crashes and falls soon after people started sleeping pills than without them; others did not.

q: Does caffeine in the morning undo the effects of a sleeping pill?
short: After a sleeping pill, morning caffeine left young men less sleepy than a dummy capsule did.

q: Do people feel more anxious or low when hungover?
short: People felt more anxious and low when hungover than when sober, and also described guilt.

q: Does anything help with the worry or low mood of a hangover?
short: No study in the review tested a way to ease hangover worry; people said sharing the hangover with friends helped.

q: What does drinking before bed do to my dream sleep?
short: After drinking, dream sleep started later and was shorter than on nights without alcohol.

q: Does a drink help me fall asleep or sleep longer?
short: On average, alcohol before bed did not help people fall asleep faster than on nights without alcohol.

q: Does caffeine during the day affect my sleep that night?
short: After caffeine, people slept about 45 minutes less than on nights without caffeine.

q: If I suddenly go without my usual caffeine, will I get a headache?
short: Without their usual caffeine, half got a headache by evening; people given caffeine pills did not.

q: Can caffeine pills in hospital stop the headache after an operation?
short: In one small trial, fewer patients given caffeine pills had headaches after surgery than patients given dummy pills.

q: What does stopping smoking feel like, and for how long?
short: After stopping smoking, people can feel grumpy, anxious and restless, and wake more at night, for weeks.

q: What is the cocaine crash, and how long does it last?
short: After a binge, people described a crash: very low mood, then long, heavy sleep and hunger.

q: How do mood, craving and sleep change after stopping cocaine?
short: In a closed research unit, men's low mood and craving were worst on the first day and eased over the next weeks.

q: Do ADHD medicines like methylphenidate make it harder for children to sleep?
short: On stimulant medicine, children took longer to fall asleep and slept less than on nights without it, sleep monitors showed.

q: Does melatonin help children on ADHD medicine fall asleep?
short: Children on ADHD medicine fell asleep about 16 minutes sooner with melatonin than with a dummy pill.

q: How do you feel the day after taking ecstasy?
short: People felt very tired and had slept less, but were not sadder than others.

q: Do people feel low a few days after taking ecstasy?
short: Two small studies disagree, so they cannot say how often a mid-week low happens.

q: Is your thinking different the day after LSD?
short: A few small changes, some better and some worse, which may just be chance.

q: Can a bad reaction to PCP last for weeks?
short: In three reported cases, a severe breakdown lasted two to four weeks, then passed.

q: Does hospital medicine shorten a long breakdown after PCP?
short: Nobody knows: in three cases, the medicines did not seem to shorten it.

q: How long does cannabis affect your driving skills?
short: For several hours; probably longer after eating it than smoking it, and longer after bigger doses.

q: Do cannabis or CBD products taken by mouth help people sleep?
short: In sleep labs, cannabis taken by mouth did not reliably change sleep, compared with a dummy pill or with sleep before treatment.

q: What happens to your sleep when you stop using a lot of cannabis?
short: Sleep got shorter and slower to start, with more dream sleep, in the first nights.

q: Does hot-pepper (capsaicin) cream ease cannabis-linked vomiting in hospital?
short: Nobody knows yet: in small studies it sometimes helped and sometimes did not.

q: Do medicines that block dopamine ease cannabis-linked vomiting in hospital?
short: In two small studies, haloperidol eased sickness more than a usual anti-sickness medicine, and people given haloperidol or droperidol went home sooner than people given other care.

q: Is the day after worse with synthetic cannabis than with ordinary cannabis?
short: People who had used both said synthetic cannabis gave a slightly worse hangover.

q: Do fentanyl test strips show fentanyl when it is there?
short: In lab tests, strips found fentanyl in 104 of 106 drug samples that had it.

q: Can a fentanyl strip show fentanyl when there is none?
short: Sometimes. Large amounts of meth, MDMA or two medicines made strips positive with no fentanyl there.

q: Do fentanyl strips pick up drugs related to fentanyl, like carfentanil?
short: In lab tests, strips found most related drugs, but not all. Carfentanil needed large amounts.

q: Do all fentanyl strips work the same?
short: No. In lab tests, brands and batches differed. Some batches needed ten times more fentanyl.

q: Do nitazene test strips work?
short: In lab tests, the strips found most nitazenes. They missed most of one group, called desnitazenes.

q: Do xylazine test strips work?
short: Strips found xylazine in 37 of 38 samples with enough of it, but often missed small amounts.

q: Do benzodiazepine strips find the newer benzodiazepines sold on the street?
short: Often not. At one drug-checking service, strips missed 9 of 24 samples with newer benzodiazepines.

q: Do colour tests like Marquis show whether a pill has MDMA in it?
short: In a lab, experts got MDMA right. Two first-time testers made many mistakes.

q: Do results with take-home strips match testing by trained staff?
short: For opioids, about the same. For meth and cocaine, take-home strips showed fentanyl far more often.

q: What can drug-checking strips and colour kits not tell you?
short: A test for one drug did not show other drugs in the mix, or how much.

q: If people are given test strips, do they use them?
short: It varies a lot. In different places, from 1 in 100 to 77 in 100.

q: What do people do when a strip shows fentanyl?
short: Some say they use less or go slower; many keep the same amount.

q: Do people throw drugs away when a test shows something unexpected?
short: Sometimes. At one festival, 67 in 100 people handed over drugs that were not as sold.

q: Do people who use test strips have fewer overdoses?
short: No one knows yet. One study found no clear difference over four weeks.

q: Do people keep using test strips over time?
short: In the one study that lasted a year, fewer people had used a strip in the past month by the end than at the start.

q: Did drug checking at a festival mean fewer hospital visits?
short: We can't tell. Fewer people were taken to hospital for drugs, but other things changed too.

q: Are people who use test strips different from people who don't?
short: Yes. In the largest US study, they more often injected and used fentanyl.

q: Can test kits do harm by making people feel falsely safe?
short: No study has measured this. Riskier use after a positive strip was rare when asked.

q: Did US states that legalised test strips see fewer drug deaths?
short: After the law, drug deaths ran about 3 a year per 100,000 people below other states' trend.

q: Do people who drink a little live longer than people who don't drink?
short: Many studies found slightly fewer deaths. Compared with people who never drank, there was no clear difference.

q: Is there an amount of alcohol with no health risk?
short: Under 40, overall risk was lowest with almost no alcohol. Over 40, one model said half to two thirds of a drink a day.

q: At what amount does drinking start to shorten life?
short: Deaths rose above about 100 grams of alcohol a week. The comparison was with very light drinking.

q: Do people who drink a little have less heart disease?
short: In many studies, people who drank a little had less heart disease than people who didn't.

q: Do gene studies back the idea that alcohol protects the heart?
short: The gene studies we read did not find that drinking a little protects the heart.

q: Do heavy drinking days change the heart risk?
short: Heavy drinking days went with more heart disease than drinking the same amount evenly.

q: Does drinking raise the risk of stroke?
short: In gene studies, more drinking went with more strokes, especially bleeding in the brain.

q: Does drinking raise blood pressure?
short: People whose genes made them drink more had higher blood pressure.

q: Does drinking raise the risk of other heart and blood-vessel problems?
short: In gene studies, more drinking went with more narrowed leg arteries; other results were unclear.

q: Does drinking alcohol raise the risk of cancer?
short: More drinking went with more mouth, throat, gullet, bowel, liver and breast cancer than not drinking.

q: Does drinking a little raise the risk of cancer?
short: Compared with not drinking, up to one drink a day went with slightly more of some cancers, fewer of others.

q: How many cancers are caused by alcohol?
short: A model estimated that drinking caused about 4 in 100 new cancers worldwide in 2020.

q: How much drinking raises the risk of liver cirrhosis?
short: The more people drank, the higher their cirrhosis risk, compared with people who did not drink.

q: Is the cirrhosis risk from drinking different for women and men?
short: At the same amount, studies found a bigger rise in cirrhosis risk for women than for men.

q: For the same amount, is drinking every day worse for the liver?
short: In one study, men who drank daily had more cirrhosis than men drinking 2 to 4 days a week.

q: How many deaths does alcohol cause worldwide?
short: Global models estimated alcohol caused about 2.3 to 2.8 million deaths a year, compared with no one drinking.

q: How common is alcohol use disorder?
short: In a US survey, 14 in 100 adults had it in the past year.

q: How many people with alcohol use disorder get help?
short: In a US survey, 20 in 100 people who ever had it sought help.

q: What are the DTs (delirium tremens), and how often do they happen?
short: Sudden confusion in alcohol withdrawal; a few in 100 people in hospital get it.

q: Do medicines prevent seizures in alcohol withdrawal?
short: In old trials, benzodiazepines cut seizures: about 1 in 100, against 8 on dummy pills.

q: Does naltrexone help people drink less?
short: On naltrexone, 46 in 100 went back to heavy drinking, against 54 on dummy pills.

q: Does acamprosate help people stop drinking?
short: In trials, 76 in 100 on acamprosate drank again, against 83 on dummy pills.

q: Do topiramate, disulfiram or other medicines help people drink less?
short: Topiramate was linked to fewer drinking days; disulfiram showed no clear benefit in blinded trials.

q: Does talking therapy add anything to naltrexone for alcohol problems?
short: In one large trial, adding talking therapy to naltrexone did not help more.

q: How many pregnant women drink alcohol?
short: About 10 in 100 pregnant women worldwide drank some alcohol. By region, from under 1 to 25.

q: How common are fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) and fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS)?
short: About 8 in 1,000 children are thought to have FASD. About 1.5 in 1,000 people have FAS.

q: How did doctors first spot fetal alcohol syndrome?
short: In 1973, doctors described 8 children of mothers who drank heavily. All grew poorly and developed slowly.

q: How much of a ketamine dose reaches the blood, and how fast?
short: Nearly all of an injected dose reaches the blood. Swallowed, only about a sixth does.

q: How much ketamine reaches the blood by nose, tongue or suppository?
short: In three men, the nose spray reached the blood best, then tongue and suppository.

q: How long does ketamine stay in the blood?
short: It drops fast at first, then falls by half every two to three hours.

q: What do brain scans show while someone is given ketamine?
short: In scans, brain activity went up, not down, most of all at the front.

q: Do the two mirror-image forms of ketamine, S and R, do different things?
short: In one small study the S form caused psychosis-like effects; the R form did not.

q: Does ketamine affect memory and thinking that night, and 3 days later?
short: That night, memory scores were far below other partygoers'. Three days later the gap was mostly gone.

q: Does using ketamine often affect memory, even days later?
short: On some memory tests, people who used ketamine most days did worse than others.

q: Does memory improve when people cut down or stop frequent ketamine use?
short: Nobody knows yet. People who had stopped did as well as people who don't use it.

q: Is using ketamine often linked to low mood, feeling detached or unusual beliefs?
short: People who used ketamine most days more often reported unusual beliefs, feeling detached or feeling low.

q: What does ketamine do to memory and attention while it is working?
short: People remembered far fewer words than on their salt-water day. An hour after it stopped, scores matched.

q: What happened when people with schizophrenia were given ketamine in a study?
short: In nine patients, symptoms rose for twenty minutes, then returned to their usual level.

q: What does ketamine do to perception, thinking and the sense of self while it is working?
short: Compared with a salt-water day, people felt cut off from themselves and their thinking got muddled.

q: How does ketamine work in the brain?
short: It blocks a docking point for the brain's main go-signal, called the NMDA receptor.

q: Do people who use cannabis often do worse on memory and thinking tests?
short: On average they score a little lower than people who use little or none.

q: Do memory and thinking differences last after people stop using cannabis?
short: Not clear. Where studies asked people to stop for over 3 days, the gap was small.

q: Does using cannabis as a teenager lower IQ later in life?
short: Not shown either way. In one study, people dependent for years lost about 6 IQ points.

q: Is teenage cannabis use linked to depression or anxiety later?
short: Teens who used cannabis the most were a bit more often depressed later than teens who didn't.

q: Is teenage cannabis use linked to suicidal thoughts or attempts?
short: Teens who used cannabis the most reported suicidal thoughts or attempts more often than teens who didn't.

q: Is using cannabis in pregnancy linked to a smaller baby, early birth or intensive care?
short: Babies were a bit lighter, and more of them went to intensive care after birth.

q: Is cannabis linked to heart attacks and strokes?
short: Some studies link it to heart attacks and strokes; a 25-year study found no link.

q: Do cannabis medicines help long-lasting pain?
short: Slightly: about half a point less pain out of 10 than with a dummy medicine.

q: Do cannabis medicines ease muscle stiffness in multiple sclerosis (MS)?
short: People felt a little less stiff than with a dummy, but doctors' tests showed no clear change.

q: Do cannabis medicines help with sickness from chemotherapy?
short: In three small trials, more people had their sickness fully controlled than with a dummy.

q: Do cannabis medicines help sleep, anxiety, appetite or other conditions?
short: Too few small trials to tell; sleep scores were slightly better than with a dummy.

q: What side effects do cannabis medicines cause?
short: More side effects than with a dummy, such as dizziness, feeling high, confusion and dry mouth.

q: How many people who use cannabis become dependent on it?
short: About 9 in 100 people who ever tried it, in two older US surveys.

q: Are frequent use and starting young linked to cannabis dependence?
short: People who use more often are more often dependent; for starting young, studies disagree.

q: How common is withdrawal when people who use cannabis regularly stop, and what is it like?
short: About 17 in 100 in general surveys; more than half in clinic and hospital groups.

q: What is cannabis hyperemesis syndrome (repeated severe vomiting), and does stopping end it?
short: Bouts of severe vomiting with regular cannabis use; in reported cases, stopping ended them.

q: How does THC move through the body after smoking and after eating, and how long does it stay in blood and urine?
short: Smoked, THC peaks in the blood within minutes; eaten, it rises slowly over hours.

q: Can cannabis cause psychosis, and does using it daily matter?
short: People who use cannabis, most of all daily, get psychosis more often than people who don't.

q: Is strong cannabis more closely linked to psychosis than weaker cannabis?
short: Daily use of strong types had the strongest link with psychosis, but the gap from weaker types could be chance.

q: Does cannabis cause psychosis, or could something else explain the link?
short: Not known. Part of the link seems to come from other differences between people.

q: Has schizophrenia become more common as more people used cannabis?
short: Studies disagree: some places saw more psychosis over time, others no rise as use grew.

q: Does how I feel beforehand change how a psychedelic trip goes?
short: Feeling calm and ready beforehand went with easier trips; feeling anxious went with more anxiety.

q: Do the place and the people around me affect a psychedelic trip?
short: In surveys, feeling safe and supported went with fewer difficult moments, by small amounts.

q: Does the kind of ayahuasca ceremony matter for how it goes?
short: People who felt safe and supported at their last ceremony recalled a little less fear.

q: How often are psychedelic trips difficult, and can problems last?
short: 41 in 100 people who had used psychedelics recalled at least one difficult trip.

q: Does music change how a psychedelic session goes?
short: Patients said music shaped their sessions; two kinds of music made no clear difference.

q: Does music change how a ketamine treatment session goes?
short: In one small trial, the top blood pressure number rose less with music.

q: Do some people feel MDMA more strongly than others?
short: In lab studies, how strong MDMA felt went most with the amount per kilo of body weight.

q: Do some people feel LSD more strongly than others?
short: In lab studies, the dose went most with how strong LSD felt. Mood and personality did too.

q: Which harm reduction services exist for benzos, and do they work?
short: Drug checking, prescribed benzos and stricter rules exist. No study has shown whether they lower harm.

q: How common is using drugs alone, and why do people do it?
short: About 3 in 4 people at harm reduction sites had used alone that week. The top reason was comfort at home.

q: Does CBD taken with THC change THC's effects?
short: Studies disagree on CBD and THC; no reliable pattern has been shown across different conditions.

q: Do drug and alcohol problems develop faster in women than in men?
short: Not shown for women in general. It was seen mostly in people in treatment.

q: Are women less likely than men to get alcohol or drug treatment?
short: For alcohol, somewhat less likely, mostly years after problems start. For drugs, about the same.

q: In drug or alcohol treatment, do women do as well as men?
short: Most large studies found no difference between women and men once in treatment.

q: Do genes and the home you grow up in shape drug problems?
short: Both are linked: what comes from birth parents, and the home a child grows up in.

q: Do words about drug use change how others see a person?
short: In one experiment, people judged 'drug use' more harshly than a 'health concern'.
topic: Stigma and the words we use

q: Does drinking at a young age lead to alcohol problems later on?
short: Not known. Some of the link seems to come from things that lead to both.

q: How often do people who use cocaine also drink or use cannabis?
short: On average, about 3 in 4 also used alcohol, and 4 to 6 in 10 cannabis.

q: Can caffeine bring on panic attacks in people with panic disorder?
short: About half had a panic attack after one big dose; none after a dummy.

q: Does eating before drinking change blood alcohol?
short: In 9 men, a meal just before drinking roughly halved peak blood alcohol.

q: Can sniffing solvents cause sudden death?
short: Sudden deaths after sniffing solvents and sprays were reported in one old survey.

q: Do official counts miss drug deaths?
short: Some deaths are missing; others are counted without showing which drug was involved.

q: Do official counts miss heroin deaths?
short: In the places studied, closer reviews linked more deaths to heroin than records did.

q: Do autopsies and drug tests change which deaths count as drug deaths?
short: Sometimes: at one centre, about 10 in 100 suspected drug deaths had another cause.

q: Does how the news describes a drug death change what readers think?
short: In one study, story details changed how harshly readers judged the person who died.

q: Did news stories about mephedrone deaths get the facts right?
short: Not always: several deaths blamed on it in the news had other causes.

q: Can drug levels change after death?
short: Yes. Levels can rise or fall and differ between blood vessels.
topic: What a test after death can show

q: Can cannabis cause a sudden death?
short: These studies do not settle that question.

q: Was mephedrone actually found in the deaths blamed on it?
short: In 25 of 128 alleged deaths, tests after death found no mephedrone.

q: Are heroin overdose deaths always caused by heroin alone?
short: Other drugs are often found. That does not show which caused the death.

q: What level of MDMA in blood is fatal?
short: These studies do not establish a fatal cutoff; the measured levels overlap.

q: Is 'excited delirium' a real cause of death?
short: The label alone does not establish what caused a death.

q: Does starting drugs young go with drug problems later?
short: People who started young more often had drug or drinking problems later on.

q: Does using cannabis lead to other drugs (the 'gateway' idea)?
short: Not known. Cannabis usually comes first, but that does not prove it leads on.

q: How common is using several drugs, and why does it matter?
short: Common among people who use illegal drugs. It makes one drug's effects hard to study.

q: Are cocaine deaths more common in hot weather, and why?
short: In 1990s New York, hot days had about a third more cocaine overdose deaths.

q: How is a death counted as a drug death?
short: Different lists use different rules, so they do not always count the same deaths.

q: Does it matter whether a coroner or a medical examiner investigates?
short: Not clear. Coroner areas recorded deaths less precisely, but switching showed no clear change.

q: Can a blood level show that a drug caused death?
short: Not on its own. Levels overlap between deaths with different causes.
topic: What a test after death can show

q: Do health workers see and treat people who use drugs differently?
short: Many health workers said they felt negative. Whether care was worse is not clear.
topic: Stigma and the words we use

q: Is the risk of dying highest just after leaving prison?
short: In one large study, the risk of dying was highest 2 to 7 days after release.

q: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment?
short: Many do. For alcohol, many people who recovered were never treated.

q: What did the 'Rat Park' studies show about environment and morphine?
short: Less than is often said. Rats living together drank less morphine water, but only in some tests.

q: Will people who use cocaine choose another reward instead?
short: Sometimes. Six people picked $5 over real cocaine doses about 1 time in 3 or 4.

q: Does believing you've had alcohol change how you act?
short: In lab tests, partly: believing they drank alcohol made men drink more.

q: How fast does cocaine act, and for how long?
short: Smoked or injected, the high peaks in about a minute and fades within 30 minutes.

q: Is crack more addictive or more harmful than powder?
short: The same drug. People starting crack reported more signs of dependence than people starting powder.

q: How quickly can dependence start after first using cocaine?
short: Within a year of starting, about 5 in 100 who used only powder were dependent; 22 in 100 who went on to crack.

q: What is levamisole in cocaine, and what harm can it do?
short: An animal worm medicine often found in cocaine, linked to blood and skin harm.

q: How common is cocaine psychosis among people treated for cocaine use?
short: 68 in 100 people treated for cocaine reported psychotic symptoms; 16 in 100 had a diagnosed disorder.

q: Do stimulant medicines help people stop using cocaine?
short: In nine trials up to 2006, they did no better than a dummy pill.

q: Why do people take ketamine, and what do they want from it?
short: Most said: for its effects, like melting into their surroundings, and for fun.

q: How much more likely are people with problem cocaine use to die?
short: Each year, 5 to 62 in 1,000 died: 4 to 8 times others their age.

q: How often is chest pain after cocaine a heart attack?
short: US studies looked at people in hospital with chest pain after cocaine. About 1 to 6 in 100 were having a heart attack.

q: Does cocaine affect memory and thinking?
short: On average, people with cocaine problems score somewhat lower on memory and attention tests.

q: Does cocaine narrow heart arteries, and do beta-blockers make it worse?
short: Yes, in a lab cocaine narrowed heart arteries a little. After a beta-blocker, blood flow fell further in all 10 patients, but its effect on heart attacks is unknown.

q: Is using ketamine linked to bladder problems?
short: Ketamine is linked to bladder problems seen in over 4,000 patients. In one survey, about 1 in 4 people who used it blamed it for urine problems.

q: How many UK deaths were linked to ketamine, and what were they?
short: In England, ketamine was found or named in 283 deaths from 1999 to 2019, about 30 a year lately. Most had other drugs found too.

q: Is ketamine as good as electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) for hard-to-treat depression?
short: Two big trials disagree: a US trial found ketamine drips at least as good as ECT. But in Swedish hospital patients, 63 in 100 got well on ECT, against 46.

q: What side effects do people have from ketamine treatment for depression?
short: With ketamine for depression, studies most often found headache and dizziness. Next came feeling unreal and higher blood pressure. Most soon passed.

q: Did teen cannabis use rise after US states legalised it?
short: Not in one big US study. After states made recreational cannabis legal, teens in school were a bit less likely to say they had used it in the past month.

q: Does a CBD medicine reduce seizures in a severe childhood epilepsy?
short: In two trials, a CBD medicine cut seizures in Dravet syndrome. Seizures at least halved in 43 to 49 in 100 children, against 26 to 27 on a dummy liquid.

q: How often do people seek emergency treatment after magic mushrooms?
short: About 2 in 1,000 people who had used magic mushrooms in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After LSD: 10 in 1,000.

q: How often do people seek emergency treatment after LSD?
short: About 10 in 1,000 people who had used LSD in the past year said they sought emergency treatment, in one big online survey. After magic mushrooms: 2 in 1,000.

q: What do people say they meet on DMT?
short: People who said they met a being on DMT mostly called it a 'being', 'guide', 'spirit' or 'alien'. People who said they met 'God' without drugs told similar stories.

q: Can a ketamine drip lift depression within hours, and for how long?
short: A ketamine drip eased depression within hours: a day later, 64 in 100 were much better, against 28 in 100 on a sedative. For most, it faded within weeks.

q: Is cannabis stronger than it used to be?
short: Yes, on average. In cannabis from 7 countries, 1970 to 2017, THC, its main active part, rose about 3 points every 10 years in weed and 6 in hash.

q: Does cannabis make people lazy or unmotivated?
short: In a London study, people using cannabis about 4 days a week felt no less motivated than people who had used it fewer than 10 times, and were as willing to work for sweets.

q: Can other people's cannabis smoke make you fail a urine drug test?
short: Rarely at the US government's workplace limit: after an hour in thick cannabis smoke, 1 of 18 people who didn't smoke went over it. At a lower limit, 12 did.

q: Can eating poppy seeds make you fail a sports drug test?
short: In one study, yes: all 9 people who ate poppy seed cake had morphine, an opioid, in their urine above the sports limit.

q: Do CBD products contain what their labels say?
short: Mostly not. Of 84 CBD products bought online in the US in 2016, only about 3 in 10 matched their CBD label. About 1 in 5 also held THC.

q: What happened after Portugal decriminalised all drugs?
short: In 2001 Portugal stopped treating having any drug for your own use, even heroin, as a crime. Drug use rose slightly; new HIV cases in people who use drugs fell.

q: Do most US dollar bills carry traces of cocaine?
short: In one US study, about 9 in 10 one-dollar bills had traces of cocaine. The typical bill held a little over a millionth of a gram.

q: Can drugs be ranked by how much harm they do?
short: Experts have tried: a UK panel ranked alcohol most harmful overall, mostly for harm to other people. For the person using, crack, heroin and meth scored worst.

q: Did the original DARE school programme stop young people using drugs?
short: No. Across 11 studies of the original DARE school classes, kids who had DARE used alcohol, tobacco and other drugs about as much as kids who didn't.

q: Did the US government's anti-drug ads stop teens using cannabis?
short: No sign they did. Congress put nearly $1 billion into the campaign, but teen cannabis use stayed flat, and teens who remembered more ads weren't less likely to start.

q: Does coffee dehydrate you?
short: Not in a 3-day test. Men who drink coffee daily peed 2.41 litres a day on coffee days and 2.43 on water days.

q: Do 'smart drugs' like Adderall make healthy people smarter?
short: Barely. A single pill of Adderall (amphetamine) or methylphenidate gave healthy adults at most a small lift on some lab tests. In one trial, people felt helped; scores didn't rise.

q: Do benzodiazepines cause dementia?
short: Not known. In Quebec health records, long use of benzodiazepines was linked to Alzheimer's. A Seattle study that tested people found no clear link with the heaviest use.

q: Why do people use kratom, and what do they say it does?
short: Mostly for pain, anxiety or depression, people told two surveys, and most felt it helped. In one, about 4 in 10 had used kratom to cut down or stop opioids.

q: How often is kratom found in overdose deaths?
short: Kratom turned up in about 6 of every 1,000 overdose deaths in 27 US states in 2016–17. It was almost always found with other drugs.

q: Does psilocybin help depression?
short: In two trials, depression scores fell more after one psilocybin session with two therapists than after a vitamin pill or a tiny dose. This was 3 to 6 weeks later.

q: Is psilocybin better than a standard antidepressant for depression?
short: Not shown. In one trial of 59 people, psilocybin and the antidepressant escitalopram showed no clear difference in depression, at 6 weeks or 6 months.

q: Does alcohol kill brain cells?
short: In one study, men who drank alcohol heavily for years had about as many nerve cells in the brain's outer layer as other men: about 23 billion each.

q: Is moderate drinking linked to changes in the brain?
short: In one UK study, people who drank more alcohol more often had a memory area rated 'shrunken' on a scan. So did 35 in 100 who barely drank.

q: Can psilocybin bring on a mystical experience, and does it last?
short: In a Johns Hopkins study, most volunteers given psilocybin scored as having a 'complete' mystical experience. Two months later, 67 in 100 ranked it among their 5 most meaningful experiences.

q: Does caffeine make you sharper, or just undo withdrawal?
short: In one lab study, caffeine made everyone faster. But those who often have it only got as alert as those who rarely do.

q: Do people describe ketamine trips the way others describe near-death experiences?
short: Of 165 drugs, ketamine trip reports used words most like accounts of near-death experiences. Salvia and LSD came close behind.

q: Can psilocybin help people drink less?
short: Maybe. In one trial, people given psilocybin with talk therapy drank heavily on about 10 in 100 days, against 24 with a comparison pill.

q: Can psilocybin help people quit smoking?
short: Not known. In one small study, 12 of 15 people given psilocybin plus lots of counselling weren't smoking 6 months later.

q: Is using LSD, mushrooms or mescaline linked to mental health problems?
short: People who had used LSD, mushrooms or mescaline reported mental health problems 2 to 3 times as often. The gap vanished once other drug use and life stress were counted.

q: Is drinking coffee linked to better or worse health?
short: Mostly better: in studies that followed people for years, people who drank coffee died a bit less often. In pregnancy, and for women's bones, the links went the other way.

q: Does giving out naloxone kits prevent opioid overdose deaths?
short: Naloxone kits are linked to fewer deaths from heroin and other opioids, but it's not proven. At least 96 in 100 people given naloxone by someone trained survived.

q: Is nitrous oxide (laughing gas) linked to nerve damage?
short: Yes: doctors have described nerve damage after nitrous oxide (laughing gas). In an online survey, about 4 in 100 people who used it in the past year reported lasting numbness.

q: Do supervised injection sites reduce overdose deaths?
short: Not proven: near Vancouver's site for injecting heroin, cocaine and other drugs, overdose deaths fell about a third after it opened. Elsewhere in the city, about a tenth.

q: Does microdosing magic mushrooms do anything, or is it placebo?
short: In two trials, people could feel a magic mushroom or LSD microdose on the day. But their mood and thinking were not clearly better than with a dummy capsule.

q: Does esketamine nasal spray work for hard-to-treat depression?
short: In two big trials, esketamine spray (a form of ketamine) did a little better than a dummy spray. Only one trial passed its main test.

q: Can touching fentanyl make you overdose?
short: Poison experts call it very unlikely for police and paramedics, and no overdose from touching fentanyl has been confirmed. In 214 news stories about exposed responders, none had proof.

q: Do police believe touching fentanyl can cause overdose? Does training change that?
short: In two US surveys at trainings, about 4 in 5 police and other responders thought touching fentanyl could make them overdose. Right after the training, far fewer did.

q: Does LSD damage your chromosomes?
short: Tests from 1967 to 1970 found no clear rise in broken chromosomes in people given pure LSD. The scare began with cells from two people in a dish.
